node_additions.label: Digital history
node_additions.date_label: Earlier roots · selected publications 2003–2022; field chronology unresolved
node_additions.description: Historical inquiry using digital media to assemble and interpret evidence, develop arguments, publish scholarship, teach and involve public audiences. This selection spans digital projects, computational exploration, preservation and source criticism, including debates over participation, race, gender and scholarly credit. Digital history overlaps with quantitative history, public history and digital humanities without being equivalent to any of them.
node_additions.scope_note: Bounded selection of projects, methods, public practice and critical reflection. No founding year, complete genealogy or comprehensive field review through 2026 is asserted.

Their 2014 methodological and collaborative account, not an independent replication of its topic-model example or a reading of either book edition. Public collaboration is presented as part of the method.
strands.works: Writing The Historian’s Macroscope in Public

strands.title: Digital History’s Perpetual Future Tense
strands.focus: Blevins recognizes digital history’s archival, pedagogical and public achievements while calling for more explicit argument-driven academic scholarship and less rhetoric of future potential. An attributed 2016 disciplinary assessment, not a field-wide quantitative audit. His later discussion explicitly recognizes interpretation in public-history projects; the distinction concerns organizing priorities, not an absence of arguments.
strands.works: Digital History’s Perpetual Future Tense

strands.title: State of the Field: Digital History
strands.focus: Romein and colleagues distinguish successive computing practices and stress that corpus composition and changing meanings constrain quantitative text analysis. Source-specific assessment, not a definition of the whole field. Digital history, computational history and digital humanities remain separate candidate identities; their relations require historical argument.
strands.works: State of the Field: Digital History

strands.title: The Transformation of Historical Research in the Digital Age
strands.focus: Milligan treats search, digitization and online scholarly practice as changes affecting ordinary historical research, not only specialist computational projects. Source-specific assessment, not a definition of the whole field. Digital history, computational history and digital humanities remain separate candidate identities; their relations require historical argument. Milligan distinguishes the field of Digital History from wider digitized historical practice and identifies public-history and quantitative traditions among its lineages. Selected section 1.3, pp. 7–8; an attributed retrospective account of plural roots, not a single founding date or an influence arrow from every earlier tradition.
strands.works: The Transformation of Historical Research in the Digital Age

strands.title: The Transnational and the Text-Searchable: Digitized Sources and the Shadows They Cast
strands.focus: Putnam examines how digitized search changes transnational research and the contextual learning formerly required by place-based work. Abstract only. Direct page access failed; no full-article or broader reception claim. Relevance spans digital and transnational history.
strands.works: The Transnational and the Text-Searchable: Digitized Sources and the Shadows They Cast

strands.title: Making a Case for the Black Digital Humanities
strands.focus: Gallon proposes Black digital humanities as a critique of racialized knowledge and a practice of historical recovery. An attributed programme within digital humanities; not an equivalence between digital humanities and digital history.
strands.works: Making a Case for the Black Digital Humanities

strands.title: Complicating a “Great Man” Narrative of Digital History in the United States
strands.focus: Leon criticizes Thomas’s digital-history genealogy for omitting women historians. Leon’s specific critique; Thomas’s chapter has not been independently read in this batch. Leon links exclusions in digital-history narratives to academic status, institutional location and the invisibility of collaborative labour. Selected chapter paragraphs, US-focused argument; her grant tallies are not independently reproduced here or adopted as this graph’s demographic baseline.
strands.works: Complicating a “Great Man” Narrative of Digital History in the United States

strands.title: Complicating a “Great Man” Narrative of Digital History in the United States
strands.focus: The AHR authors report expanding their account after reading Leon’s intervention. Authors’ documented acknowledgement during revision, not proof of field-wide influence or a date for final publication.
strands.works: Complicating a “Great Man” Narrative of Digital History in the United States

strands.title: Web archives and (digital) history: a troubled past and a promising future?
strands.focus: Winters distinguishes the broad practices of digital history from historians’ more limited engagement with web archives and digital preservation. Repository manuscript pp. 4–6; her 2018 assessment, not a current census or an equivalence between digital history, web history and digital humanities. Winters warns that curated access routes can privilege particular kinds of web evidence and shape the histories researchers write. Repository manuscript pp. 7–9, selected British Library/Archive-It examples; no global archive-coverage estimate or present-day collection count.
strands.works: Web archives and (digital) history: a troubled past and a promising future?

node_additions.label: Web history / Archived-web research
node_additions.date_label: Earlier roots · selected publications 2003–2026; field chronology unresolved
node_additions.description: Historical inquiry into the web and inquiry using archived web evidence. These overlap but differ: web archives also inform political, social and cultural histories whose object is not the web itself. Archival and information scholars contribute contextual methods without being assigned an exclusive historian profession.
node_additions.scope_note: Bounded selection of projects, methods, public practice and critical reflection. No founding year, complete genealogy or comprehensive field review through 2026 is asserted.

representative_people.context: Hegarty attributes gaps and uneven access in Australian social-media archives to different collection strategies and changing platform constraints. Indexed author abstract only; two Australian library cases. No detailed findings beyond that abstract, and no claim that all national archives behave alike. Hegarty explicitly adapts Ann Stoler’s attention to archival form and placement to interpreting platform-mediated web collections. Indexed author abstract only; specifically attributed methodological use, not a general Stoler-to-web-history influence arrow or a new reading of Stoler’s book.
representative_people.works: Web archives after platformization: reading social media collections along the archival grain

representative_people.context: Gibbons presents mediated recordkeeping and platform paradata as ways to document how archival processes shape evidential meaning. Selected introduction/conclusion. The model originated in earlier doctoral research; the 2026 paper presents a diagnostic framework, not a field-tested institutional implementation. Gibbons argues that making archival gaps visible cannot itself redistribute authority or settle Indigenous sovereignty and community-governance questions. Selected limitations/conclusion; a stated boundary of the model, not a claim that technical documentation delivers justice or substitutes for Indigenous-led decisions.
